messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David, a 46-year-old graphic designer, presented for treatment eight months after an incident that he felt had cleaved his life in two. Before that Saturday, he described his life as ordered and meaningful; now, he felt adrift in a constant state of alert. The event itself was a blur of chaos. He had been photographing a street festival downtown when a protest march unexpectedly converged with the crowd. Fights broke out, and police moved in. David was trying to leave the area when he saw an officer strike a young man with a baton, opening a deep, bleeding gash above the man’s eye. The image was seared into his mind. Moments later, mistaken for a rioter, David was thrown to the ground by two officers. He remembers the rough texture of the pavement against his cheek and a profound sense of powerlessness.

In the weeks that followed, the memory refused to settle into a coherent story. When he tried to explain what happened to his wife, he reported that the words would get stuck; he would lose the thread, overwhelmed by a surge of panic that forced him to stop talking. The memory was not a narrative but a series of sensory fragments that could be triggered without warning. A siren in the distance, the sight of a police car parked outside a coffee shop—these would instantly bring back the feeling of the pavement on his skin. He began altering his driving routes to avoid the precinct near his home. The most potent trigger, however, was seeing injuries. Watching an action movie where a character was cut, or even seeing a child with a scraped knee at the park, would plunge him back into the moment he saw the gash on the young man’s face.

To manage these intrusions, David began to systematically fill every moment of silence. Working from home provided the perfect environment for this. He kept podcasts playing constantly, from the moment he woke up until he went to bed, a wall of sound to keep his own unwanted thoughts at bay. When the noise wasn't enough, he would lose himself for hours scrolling through design forums or playing mindless games on his phone, long after his work for the day was done. He started declining invitations from friends, avoiding the unpredictability of other people and their conversations. His world shrank to his home office, his screen a shield against the intrusive memories.

Despite these efforts, his body remained on high alert. He described a constant, humming tension in his shoulders and jaw, a feeling that he had to be ready to react to danger at any moment. Even at home, a place he knew was safe, he found he was unable to relax. If his wife suggested they go out to a new restaurant, his first instinct was to look up the floor plan online, identifying all possible escape routes before he could even consider the menu. The feeling of being trapped was intolerable.

This constant vigilance and avoidance began to corrode his life. His freelance business suffered as he missed deadlines, his focus fractured by the need to keep his mind perpetually occupied. The injustice of the event gnawed at him; the officers faced no repercussions, and this fact made everything else feel pointless. He came to believe that his life had been destroyed by those few minutes on the pavement. Nothing felt meaningful anymore—not his work, which he once loved, nor his relationships. The final impetus for seeking therapy was when his wife told him, with tears in her eyes, that she felt like she was living with a ghost. David is now hoping to find a way to quiet the constant alarm bells in his head, but he holds a deep fear that the man he was before the incident is gone for good.
